subject: chemistry
title: Benzene and electrophilic substitution
key_idea: Benzene is a planar ring with a delocalised π system, which makes it unusually stable. It therefore keeps its ring and undergoes electrophilic substitution, not addition. Nitration, halogenation and Friedel–Crafts reactions all replace an H atom with an electrophile.

blocks.text: Benzene has the formula C₆H₆. This section covers the Kekulé model and the delocalised model.

items.meaning: A ring of six carbons with alternating single and double bonds: cyclohexa-1,3,5-triene.
The p electrons are shared around the whole ring in a π system, above and below the plane of the ring.

items: The ring is **planar**, with bond angles of 120°.
Each carbon forms three σ bonds, to two carbons and one hydrogen.
Each carbon has one p orbital left over, pointing up and down from the ring.
The six p orbitals overlap sideways, forming a ring of delocalised π electrons above and below the plane.
All the carbon–carbon bonds are the same length, **between** a single and a double bond.

blocks.text: Benzene can be drawn as a hexagon with alternating double bonds, or as a hexagon with an inner circle for the delocalised electrons.

items: Benzene is a planar ring of six carbons with delocalised π electrons.
All the C–C bonds are equal in length.
The Kekulé structure is a simpler, older model.

blocks.text: Experiments show that benzene does not match the Kekulé structure. Three pieces of evidence support delocalisation.

rows: Three long single bonds (0.153 nm) and three short double bonds (0.134 nm)
All six bonds are equal, about 0.140 nm
No reaction with bromine water; substitution occurs

diagram.alt: Practise calculating the extra stability of benzene from enthalpies of hydrogenation.
diagram.question: The enthalpy of hydrogenation of cyclohexene is **−{e} kJ/mol**. That of benzene is **−{b} kJ/mol**. Calculate how much more stable benzene is than cyclohexa-1,3,5-triene, in kJ/mol.

items: Benzene is **more stable** than the hypothetical cyclohexa-1,3,5-triene, because its π electrons are delocalised.
More energy would be needed to break the delocalised system, so benzene is less reactive than the Kekulé structure suggests.
Equal bond lengths show there are no separate single and double bonds.
Hydrogenation is about 150 kJ/mol less exothermic than predicted, so benzene is extra stable.
Benzene does not decolourise bromine water.

sections.heading: Why benzene substitutes rather than adds

blocks.text: Benzene resists bromination, unlike alkenes. This section explains why, in terms of electron density.

items: An alkene has a **localised** π bond between two carbons. The electron density is high.
This density polarises an approaching Br₂ molecule, so the alkene adds bromine without a catalyst.
Benzene's π electrons are spread over six carbons. The electron density between any two carbons is **lower**.
Benzene cannot polarise Br₂ enough to react.
Addition would destroy the stable delocalised ring. **Substitution** keeps the ring intact.
Alkene: localised π bond, high electron density, adds bromine.
Benzene: delocalised, lower density, no reaction without a catalyst.
Benzene substitutes so that it keeps its delocalised ring.

blocks.text: Aromatic compounds are named with the benzene ring as the base. Number the ring to give the substituents the lowest locants.

items: One substituent: no number needed, e.g. nitrobenzene, chlorobenzene, methylbenzene.
Two or more: number the positions, alphabetically if there is a choice, e.g. 1-chloro-2-nitrobenzene.
Use prefixes di, tri for repeats: 2,4,6-tribromophenol, 2,4-dinitromethylbenzene.
Where a group gives the ring a special name, that group is at position 1: 3-nitrobenzoic acid, 2-nitrophenol.
As a substituent, C₆H₅– is called **phenyl**.
Use the lowest numbers for the substituents.
Acid and phenol groups sit at position 1 in their names.

blocks.text: In each reaction an electrophile replaces a hydrogen atom on the ring. Pick a reaction to see the reagents, the electrophile and the product.

options.label: Chlorination
results: Cl₂ with AlCl₃ (or Fe) as halogen carrier, room temperature

options.label: Bromination
results: Br₂ with FeBr₃ (or AlBr₃) as halogen carrier, room temperature

options.label: Friedel–Crafts alkylation
results: Haloalkane, e.g. CH₃Cl, with AlCl₃, heat

options.label: Friedel–Crafts acylation
results: Acyl chloride, e.g. CH₃COCl, with AlCl₃, heat

items.text: Two electrons from the delocalised π system form a bond to the electrophile, E⁺.
A positively charged intermediate forms. The ring is no longer fully delocalised, and the carbon attacked has both H and E.
The C–H bond breaks. The electrons return to the ring and delocalisation is restored.
H⁺ reacts with the anion: H⁺ + AlCl₄⁻ → HCl + AlCl₃ (or H⁺ + HSO₄⁻ → H₂SO₄).

items: The halogen carrier (AlCl₃, AlBr₃, FeBr₃, or iron) is a **catalyst**. It is regenerated.
Friedel–Crafts reactions are important in synthesis because they form a new **C–C bond** to the ring.
Nitration is important in synthesis: nitrobenzene is reduced to phenylamine (used for dyes and drugs), and nitration is used to make explosives.
Only one substituent is added in each reaction here (monosubstitution).
The electrophile is attacked by the π electrons, then H⁺ is lost.
The catalyst makes the electrophile and is regenerated.
Friedel–Crafts reactions build a C–C bond onto the ring.

checks.q: The enthalpy of hydrogenation of cyclohexene is −120 kJ/mol and of benzene is −208 kJ/mol. Explain what these values show about the structure of benzene.
checks.a: Three C=C bonds in the Kekulé structure would give 3 × −120 = −360 kJ/mol. The actual value is 152 kJ/mol less exothermic, so benzene is more stable than the Kekulé structure. This is because the π electrons are delocalised.

checks.q: Explain why benzene does not decolourise bromine water but cyclohexene does.
checks.a: Cyclohexene has a localised π bond with high electron density, which polarises Br₂ and allows addition. Benzene's π electrons are delocalised, so the electron density between carbons is lower. It cannot polarise Br₂ enough to react.

checks.q: Write equations to show how the electrophile forms, and outline the mechanism, for the nitration of benzene.
checks.a: HNO₃ + 2H₂SO₄ → NO₂⁺ + H₃O⁺ + 2HSO₄⁻. The π electrons of the ring attack NO₂⁺, giving a positively charged intermediate. H⁺ is lost from the carbon with the NO₂, restoring the delocalised ring and forming nitrobenzene. The H⁺ reacts with HSO₄⁻ to reform H₂SO₄.

blocks.text: This part covers unfamiliar reactions and the electrophile in halogenation.

items: For halogenation, the electrophile can be assumed to be X⁺.
Halogen carriers include iron, iron halides and aluminium halides.
Unfamiliar electrophilic substitutions can appear with extra information. Use the same pattern: find the electrophile, show the attack, then the loss of H⁺.
The nitration mechanism must include the equations that form NO₂⁺.

blocks.text: This part covers the reactions of benzene in the specification, including combustion.

items: Benzene burns in air with a **smoky flame**, because it has a high proportion of carbon, giving soot (carbon) from incomplete combustion.
Bromination uses bromine with a catalyst, such as FeBr₃ or AlBr₃.
Friedel–Crafts uses a halogenoalkane or an acyl chloride with aluminium chloride as catalyst.
Either the Kekulé or the delocalised structure may be used in equations and mechanisms.

blocks.text: This part covers the mechanisms to outline and the uses of the reactions.

items: Outline the mechanisms for nitration, including the nitronium ion NO₂⁺, and acylation using AlCl₃ as catalyst.
Substitution is limited to monosubstitution.
Use enthalpies of hydrogenation as thermochemical evidence for the extra stability.
Explain why substitution occurs in preference to addition: addition would destroy the delocalised π system.
Nitration is used to make explosives, and nitro compounds are reduced to amines.

blocks.text: This part covers hybridisation, methylbenzene reactions and side-chain halogenation.

items: Each carbon is **sp²** hybridised. The three sp² orbitals form σ bonds to two carbons and one hydrogen, in a plane at 120°.
The unhybridised p orbitals overlap sideways to give the delocalised π system above and below the ring.
Two mechanism types appear: electrophilic substitution (here) and addition–elimination (acyl chlorides).
Halogenation: Cl₂ or Br₂ with AlCl₃ or AlBr₃ gives halogenoarenes. Methylbenzene gives a mixture of 2- and 4-halogenomethylbenzene.
Nitration: concentrated HNO₃ and concentrated H₂SO₄, at 25–60 °C.
Friedel–Crafts alkylation: CH₃Cl and AlCl₃, heat. Acylation: CH₃COCl and AlCl₃, heat.
Side-chain oxidation: hot alkaline KMnO₄, then dilute acid, gives benzoic acid.
Hydrogenation of the ring: H₂ with Pt or Ni, heat, gives a cyclohexane ring.

rows: Halogen carrier (AlCl₃ or AlBr₃), in the dark, room temperature
UV light or boiling, no halogen carrier

blocks.text: Chlorobenzene is far less reactive than chloroethane in substitution reactions. A lone pair on chlorine is delocalised into the ring, so the C–Cl bond is stronger.
